Empirical Research Plan  
“Do high stock prices stimulate investment in equity-dependent firms?”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Method: Difference-in-Differences (two-way fixed effects), complemented by an
instrumental-variables (2SLS) robustness test.

Why DiD?  
• We have panel data that allow us to compare the investment of equity-dependent
  firms (“treatment group”) with otherwise similar but less equity-dependent
  firms (“control group”).  
• Stock-market–wide price run-ups/crashes are plausibly exogenous to any one
  firm’s current investment opportunities. These aggregate valuation shocks
  provide the time-series “switch‐on / switch-off” required for DiD.  
• Two-way fixed effects absorb all time-invariant firm characteristics and all
  economy-wide shocks, leaving the interaction between equity dependence and
  the shock as the causal object.

Why an IV robustness test?  
• Residual concerns that aggregate shocks might still correlate with investment
  opportunities can be addressed by instrumenting each firm’s stock price with
  an exogenous component – e.g., the leave-one-out industry return – and
  estimating 2SLS within the same panel framework.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
  Treat_it = EquityDependent_i × Shock_t

EquityDependent_i (ED):  
  = 1 if the firm’s Kaplan–Zingales (or similar) index of financing need is in
  the top tercile during a pre-sample window (1980-1982), 0 otherwise.

Exogenous valuation shock (Shock_t):  
  = 1 for calendar quarters in which the equal-weighted CRSP market return is
  in the top (or bottom) quintile of the entire 1980–1999 distribution, 0
  otherwise.  Results are symmetric if we separate positive and negative shocks.

Control group  
  • Non-ED firms in any quarter, plus ED firms in non-shock quarters form the
    counterfactual.  DiD therefore uses within-firm changes and cross-firm
    contrasts simultaneously.

Treatment timing  
  Quarterly.  The “event” starts on the first day of a shock quarter and ends
  on the last.  We can refine to monthly horizon for robustness.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends  
    In the absence of valuation shocks, capital-expenditure trends for ED and
    non-ED firms would be the same.  Plausibility: Both groups are public U.S.
    firms exposed to the same macro cycle; firm and year FEs bolster this.

A2. Exogeneity of aggregate valuation shocks  
    Aggregate market moves are unrelated to any one firm’s current investment
    opportunity set.  Large macro or monetary surprises are overwhelmingly
    driven by factors outside individual firms’ capex plans.

A3. Stable group membership / no manipulation  
    Firms cannot move from non-ED to ED status in response to contemporaneous
    shocks because ED is pre-computed and time-invariant.

A4. No spillovers  
    One firm’s investment response does not materially influence another
    firm’s stock price within the same quarter at the market-wide level.

A5. First-stage relevance (for IV robustness)  
    Industry-wide return shocks predict individual stock prices strongly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Differential sensitivity to the business cycle  
    If ED firms are systematically in younger, high-growth industries, their
    investment may be more pro-cyclical.  
    → Mitigation: Add industry-year fixed effects and controls for sales
      growth, cash flow, and Tobin’s Q.  Also run event-study graphs to confirm
      parallel pre-trends.

T2. Contamination of shocks by fundamentals  
    A “bull” quarter might coincide with genuinely better investment
    opportunities.  
    → Mitigation: (i) Use only the residual component of market returns that
      is orthogonal to macro fundamentals (e.g., regress market return on
      GDP-growth surprises, Fed funds changes; keep residual).  
      (ii) IV approach: instrument firm-level price with leave-one-out
      industry return (industry_j,t excluding firm i).

T3. Anticipation / lagged adjustment  
    Firms may file capex plans before the valuation shock materialises.  
    → Mitigation: (i) Use high-frequency shocks (monthly) and measure capex
      over the following four quarters.  
      (ii) Include leads of the treatment interaction in the regression; lack
      of significant pre-effects supports no anticipation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # TWFE and IV estimation
library(lmtest)       # coeftest / wald tests
library(sandwich)     # vcovCL for clustering

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# ------------------------------------------------------
df <- fread("firm_panel_1980_1999.csv")   # one row = firm-quarter

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# ------------------------------------------------------
# Capital expenditures scaled by lagged PPE
df[, capex_ratio := CAPEX / shift(PPE, 1, type = "lag"), by = firm_id]

# Equity dependence: compute in pre-period and keep fixed
pre <- df[year <= 1982,
          .(ED_index = mean(KZ_index, na.rm = TRUE)), 
          by = firm_id]
cutoff <- quantile(pre$ED_index, probs = .67, na.rm = TRUE)
pre[, ED := as.integer(ED_index > cutoff)]
df <- merge(df, pre[, .(firm_id, ED)], by = "firm_id", all.x = TRUE)

# Market valuation shock
# First create quarterly market return
mkt <- df[, .(mkt_ret = mean(MKT_RET)), by = .(year, qtr)]
thresh <- quantile(mkt$mkt_ret, probs = .80)      # top quintile
mkt[, Shock := as.integer(mkt_ret >= thresh)]
df <- merge(df, mkt[, .(year, qtr, Shock)], by = c("year","qtr"))

# Treatment indicator
df[, Treat := ED * Shock]

# Controls
df[, controls := .(log_assets = log(ASSETS),
                   cashflow = OCF / ASSETS,
                   sales_growth = (SALES - shift(SALES,1,type="lag")) /
                                   shift(SALES,1,type="lag")),
   by = firm_id]

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DiD specification
# CAPEX_it = β * Treat_it + γ X_it + α_i + δ_t + ε_it
# ------------------------------------------------------
did <- feols(capex_ratio ~ Treat + cashflow + sales_growth + log_assets | 
               firm_id + year_q, 
             data = df, 
             cluster = ~firm_id)

summary(did)

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 4. IV robustness: instrument log(stock price) with leave-one-out industry return
# ------------------------------------------------------
df[, ind_ret := mean(STOCK_RET), by = .(sic2, year, qtr)]
df[, loo_ind_ret := ind_ret - STOCK_RET]   # leave one out
iv <- feols(capex_ratio ~ log(MB) + cashflow + sales_growth + log_assets | 
              firm_id + year_q | log(MB) ~ loo_ind_ret,
            data = df, cluster = ~firm_id)
summary(iv)

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Placebo pre-trend test
# ------------------------------------------------------
df[, Treat_lead2 := shift(Treat, 2, type = "lead"), by = firm_id]

placebo <- feols(capex_ratio ~ Treat_lead2 + cashflow + sales_growth +
                   log_assets | firm_id + year_q,
                 data = df, cluster = ~firm_id)
summary(placebo)
```

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Theory predicts β > 0:  A $1 rise in “non-fundamental” stock price should
relax equity-dependent firms’ financing constraints, increasing investment.
Prior work suggests an elasticity around 0.1–0.2: a 10 % higher valuation
raises capex by roughly 1–2 % of beginning-of-period PPE.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1. Parallel pre-trends visually verified ................. 1  
C2. No anticipation (placebo leads insignificant) .......... 1  
C3. Stable treatment assignment (ED measured pre-period) ... 1  
C4. No spillovers or interference .......................... 0.5  
C5. Correct standard-error clustering (firm-level) ......... 1  

Total ≈ 4.5 / 5.  Overall, identification is plausible but
still hinges on aggregate shocks being orthogonal to firm-level
investment opportunities.
